questions.q: The radius of a nucleus of mass number $A$ is proportional to:
questions.solution:
$R = R_{0}A^{1/3}$ with $R_{0} = 1.2$ fm.

Since volume $\propto R^{3} \propto A$, the **density of nuclear matter is the same for every nucleus** — about $2.3 \times 10^{17}$ kg/m$^{3}$.

Nucleons pack like marbles in a bag: more marbles, bigger bag, same packing.

questions.q: The mass of a nucleus is always:
questions.solution:
The nucleus weighs **less**, and the missing mass $\Delta m$ has become the binding energy, $E = \Delta m c^{2}$.

To take the nucleus apart you must supply exactly that energy — which is the same as buying the missing mass back.
options: greater than the sum of its nucleons' masses
less than the sum of its nucleons' masses

questions.q: The binding energy per nucleon is greatest for nuclei of mass number around:
questions.solution:
The curve peaks near $A \approx \mathbf{56}$ — iron and nickel, the most tightly bound nuclei there are.

Everything lighter can release energy by **fusion**, everything heavier by **fission**, and both roads lead towards iron. It is why iron is the end of the line inside a dying star.

questions.q: Two nuclei are isotopes if they have the same:
questions.solution:
**Isotopes** share the atomic number $Z$ — the same element, different numbers of neutrons.

Isobars share the mass number $A$; isotones share the neutron number.

questions.q: The half-life of a radioactive sample is $T$. After $3T$, the fraction remaining is:
questions.solution:
Each half-life halves what is left: $\tfrac12 \to \tfrac14 \to \mathbf{\tfrac18}$.

Decay never quite reaches zero — it is exponential, so it always halves and never runs out on paper.

questions.q: A radioactive sample has a half-life of $10$ days. Starting from $80$ g, find the mass (in g) remaining after $30$ days.
Find the radius (in fm) of a nucleus with $A = 27$, taking $R_{0} = 1.2$ fm.
Find the energy equivalent (in MeV) of a mass defect of $0.002$ u. Take $1$ u $= 931$ MeV/c$^{2}$, correct to three decimal places.
questions.solution:
$E = 0.002 \times 931 = \mathbf{1.862}$ MeV.

The conversion $1\text{ u} = 931$ MeV is the workhorse of this chapter — worth committing to memory.

questions.q: A sample has a half-life of $693$ s. Find its decay constant, in units of $10^{-3}$ s$^{-1}$. Take $\log_{e}2 = 0.693$.
questions.solution:
$\lambda = \dfrac{0.693}{T_{1/2}} = \dfrac{0.693}{693} = 1 \times 10^{-3}$ s$^{-1}$.

So the answer is $\mathbf{1}$ (in units of $10^{-3}$ s$^{-1}$).

questions.q: A nucleus of mass number $16$ has a binding energy per nucleon of $8$ MeV. Find its total binding energy, in MeV.
questions.solution:
$BE = 16 \times 8 = \mathbf{128}$ MeV.

Oxygen-16 really is close to this — one of the most tightly bound of the light nuclei.

questions.q: Sketch in words the graph of binding energy per nucleon against mass number, and use it to explain why both fission and fusion release energy.
questions.solution:
**The shape.** The curve rises steeply for light nuclei, reaching about $8.8$ MeV per nucleon near $A = 56$, then falls slowly to about $7.6$ MeV per nucleon at $A = 238$.

A **higher** binding energy per nucleon means a **more stable** nucleus.

**Fission.** A heavy nucleus ($A \approx 240$, about $7.6$ MeV per nucleon) splits into two middling ones ($A \approx 120$, about $8.5$ MeV per nucleon). Each nucleon becomes more tightly bound, and the difference — roughly $0.9$ MeV per nucleon, so around $200$ MeV in total — is released.

**Fusion.** Two very light nuclei join to make one that sits higher on the steeply rising part of the curve, again releasing the difference. Per nucleon fusion releases even more than fission, which is why the Sun outperforms any reactor.

Both processes move nuclei **towards $A = 56$**, which is the deepest valley of stability — energy is released whenever matter rolls downhill towards iron.

questions.q: State the law of radioactive decay and derive the relation between half-life and decay constant.
questions.solution:
**The law.** The rate of decay is proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei present:

$-\dfrac{dN}{dt} = \lambda N$.

**Solving.** Separate and integrate:

$\dfrac{dN}{N} = -\lambda\,dt \Rightarrow \log_{e}\dfrac{N}{N_{0}} = -\lambda t \Rightarrow \mathbf{N = N_{0}e^{-\lambda t}}$.

**Half-life.** Put $N = \dfrac{N_{0}}{2}$ at $t = T_{1/2}$:

$\tfrac12 = e^{-\lambda T_{1/2}} \Rightarrow \lambda T_{1/2} = \log_{e}2$.

$\mathbf{T_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{\lambda}}$.

Decay is purely statistical: no individual nucleus ages or is 'due'. Which one goes next is unknowable, yet the behaviour of a mole of them is exactly predictable.

questions.q: Distinguish between nuclear fission and nuclear fusion, with an example of each, and explain why fusion is so much harder to achieve on Earth.
questions.solution:
**Fission.** A heavy nucleus splits into two lighter ones, usually after absorbing a neutron, releasing about $200$ MeV and two or three more neutrons — which is what makes a chain reaction possible.

$^{235}_{92}\text{U} + ^{1}_{0}\text{n} \to ^{141}_{56}\text{Ba} + ^{92}_{36}\text{Kr} + 3\,^{1}_{0}\text{n} + Q$

**Fusion.** Two light nuclei join to make a heavier one, releasing energy — about $17.6$ MeV for the deuterium–tritium reaction, and far more **per nucleon** than fission.

$^{2}_{1}\text{H} + ^{3}_{1}\text{H} \to ^{4}_{2}\text{He} + ^{1}_{0}\text{n} + 17.6\text{ MeV}$

**Why fusion is hard.** Both nuclei are positively charged, so they repel fiercely, and they must be brought within about $10^{-15}$ m for the strong force to take over.

That needs temperatures of the order of $10^{7}$ K and enormous pressure — conditions the Sun's gravity supplies for free and no laboratory can hold for long.

Fission needs no such threshold: a slow neutron is uncharged and simply walks into the nucleus.

questions.q: Calculate the binding energy of a helium nucleus, given: mass of proton $= 1.00728$ u, neutron $= 1.00867$ u, helium nucleus $= 4.00151$ u, and $1$ u $= 931$ MeV.
questions.solution:
**Sum of the free nucleons' masses** ($2$ protons, $2$ neutrons):

$2(1.00728) + 2(1.00867) = 2.01456 + 2.01734 = 4.03190$ u.

**Mass defect:**

$\Delta m = 4.03190 - 4.00151 = 0.03039$ u.

**Binding energy:**

$BE = 0.03039 \times 931 \approx \mathbf{28.3}$ MeV.

**Per nucleon:** $\dfrac{28.3}{4} \approx 7.1$ MeV — unusually high for so light a nucleus, which is exactly why the alpha particle is so stable and why alpha decay happens at all.

questions.q: State three properties of the nuclear force.
questions.solution:
1. **Strongest of the known forces** — about $100$ times stronger than the electrostatic repulsion it has to overcome inside a nucleus.

2. **Extremely short range** — effective only within a few femtometres. Beyond that it falls away to nothing, which is why very large nuclei become unstable: every proton repels every other across the whole nucleus, but only neighbours attract.

3. **Charge independent** — the force between two protons, two neutrons, or a proton and a neutron is essentially the same. It acts on nucleons as nucleons, not as charges.

4. It **saturates**: each nucleon interacts only with its immediate neighbours, which is why binding energy per nucleon is roughly constant rather than growing with $A$.
